lectures.title: Privacy Coins: Monero and Zcash - lesson synthesis
Privacy Coins: Monero and Zcash - assigned reading

questions.question_stem: Why do day 6's co-spend heuristic and change heuristic have nothing to work on in a Monero trace?
questions.correct_answer: Inputs hide among decoys, outputs are one-time keys and amounts are hidden, so there is no public graph to follow.
incorrect_answers: Monero has no public ledger, so no transaction can be read and nothing in it can be quoted from a block.
Monero lets each user choose privacy, so only the shielded payments break both of them and the rest still work.
Monero addresses change every block, so a cluster built from them is out of date before it can be used.
questions.explanation: Monero hides sender, receiver and amount by default for everyone, so there is no transparent part. The ledger is still public: time, fee and shape can be quoted.
questions.lesson_block: Monero hides sender, receiver and amount

specific_source.anchor: Monero hides sender, receiver and amount

questions.question_stem: A Monero ring has 16 members, and one output also appears as a decoy in 20 other rings. What does that say about who spent it?
questions.correct_answer: Nothing: appearing often as a decoy says nothing about who spent the output.
incorrect_answers: It was spent in the first ring, since the first ring to list it holds its spend.
It was spent in one of the 21 rings, since an output seen often gets spent often.
It belongs to the ring's signer, since the most repeated member signs the ring.
questions.explanation: A ring signature proves one member signed, not which. The analyst writes 'one of 16' and does not pick one on a hunch.
questions.lesson_block: A ring hides the spender among 15 decoys

specific_source.anchor: A ring hides the spender among 15 decoys

questions.question_stem: What does a Monero key image let the network do?
questions.correct_answer: Refuse a second spend of the same output without showing which ring member was the real one.
incorrect_answers: Show which ring member was spent, so an analyst can mark the real input after the fact is over.
Reveal the sender's address to nodes, so each node can check the signature right away.
Hide the fee from observers, so that only the sender and the receiver can see what it cost.
questions.explanation: Each real output gives one key image when spent. A repeat is refused, so double-spends fail while the spent output stays hidden among the ring.

questions.question_stem: A ransom note gives a Monero address, and a search for it on a block explorer finds nothing. How should the analyst read that?
questions.correct_answer: A Monero address never appears on chain, because payments go to one-time keys, so it is an off-chain lead.
incorrect_answers: The ransom was never paid, because a paid address always shows its payments on a block explorer page.
The explorer is out of date, because a Monero address is listed once its first payment confirms.
The address is a Zcash z-address, because only shielded addresses are missing from the explorers that analysts use.
questions.explanation: The slide says a Monero 'address' from a seized wallet or ransom note is never found on chain. The address is a lead for an exchange account or wallet file, not a search term.

questions.question_stem: A Monero transaction at 14:02 has a fee and two outputs. What can the analyst's note state about it?
questions.correct_answer: That it happened, when, its fee and its shape, but nothing about who paid whom or how much was paid.
incorrect_answers: Who paid whom and how much, because the ledger shows both for the first transaction in each block.
Nothing, because Monero transactions are not recorded on a public ledger an analyst can read.
The sender and the amount only, because Monero hides just the recipient by default for payments.
questions.explanation: Transaction ID, block, time, fee, counts of inputs and outputs, ring members and key images are public. The real ring member, the recipient and the amounts are hidden.

questions.question_stem: An analyst has a Monero transaction from 2016 and another from 2023. How should the analyst treat the 'newest ring member is real' guess?
questions.correct_answer: As a finding about early Monero; it should not be applied to the 2023 transaction without a newer study.
incorrect_answers: As a rule that holds for every Monero transaction, because users always spend their newest coins first of all.
As false for both, because Monero has always drawn its decoys to match real spending behavior.
As true for 2023 and false for 2016, because larger rings make the newest member likelier to be real.
questions.explanation: The 2018 study found the newest member was real about 80% of the time in early Monero. Rings have since grown to 16 members, so the date of the transaction decides what can be said.

specific_source.anchor: Old Monero leaked: zero decoys, newest is real

questions.question_stem: Why did early Monero inputs with no decoys also weaken other users' privacy?
questions.correct_answer: A spent output they named could be struck from other rings, leaving those easier to trace.
incorrect_answers: They revealed the sender's view key, so every transaction of that sender could then be read.
They were signed twice, so the second signature revealed all the other members of every ring.
They came only from miners, so any ring that held one named a miner as its real spender every time.
questions.explanation: About 62% of inputs with decoys were traceable by this chain reaction. The fixes were a minimum number of decoys and then rings of 16.

questions.question_stem: A ransom is paid to a Zcash t-address and then sent t → z. Where does the trace stop, and what does the ledger still show?
questions.correct_answer: It stops at the shielding transaction, which shows the sending address and the amount going into the pool.
incorrect_answers: It stops at the t-address, because a t-address itself hides the sender and the amount of a payment.
It does not stop, because shielded transfers show the receiving z-address and the amount of each one of them.
It stops before the t → z transaction, because shielding transactions are not recorded on the chain.
questions.explanation: t → t works like Bitcoin, t → z shows one side and stops there, z → z shows only that a transaction happened and its fee, and z → t picks the trace up again.
questions.lesson_block: Zcash has two pools: one public, one shielded

specific_source.anchor: Zcash has two pools: one public, one shielded

questions.question_stem: What makes tracing Zcash different from tracing Monero?
questions.correct_answer: Zcash hides data only inside its shielded pool, so transparent transfers trace like Bitcoin, while Monero hides everything.
incorrect_answers: Zcash hides data for every transaction by default, while Monero lets each user pick a transparent transfer if asked.
Zcash hides only the sender, while Monero hides only the receiver and the amount of each payment on the full chain.
Zcash can be traced like Bitcoin throughout, because anyone with a block explorer can read its shielded pool in full.
questions.explanation: Name the coin first. Monero has no public part; Zcash has transparent t-addresses and shielded z-addresses, and the address type tells the analyst which rules apply.

specific_source.anchor: Zcash has two pools: one public, one shielded

questions.question_stem: The same unique amount is shielded at block 100 and deshielded at block 104. How should the analyst word this?
questions.correct_answer: As a lead, Low: amount and timing alone match, which suggests a link but does not establish one.
incorrect_answers: As a link, High: a unique amount returning within a few blocks proves one owner of both.
As a link, Moderate: matching amounts are one strong line on the same ledger and so count as such.
As nothing, because a z → t transaction never reveals an amount that could be compared to the first.
questions.explanation: The 2018 study linked deposits and withdrawals this way. On the course scale, amount and timing alone are Low, so the match is a lead for an agent.

questions.question_stem: A colleague quotes 'a study linked 28.5% of all Zcash ever deposited' as a fact about Zcash today. What is wrong with that?
questions.correct_answer: The figure describes use up to January 2018, so it needs its date and a newer study.
incorrect_answers: Nothing, because a published percentage from a Zcash study holds as long as the coin does.
It describes Monero, because only Monero has been studied for round trips of this kind.
It is too low, because the study left out most of the early deposits the miners made.
questions.explanation: The study's data run to January 2018, when most activity was transparent and miners and founders had to shield new coins. Facts that change carry an as-of date.

questions.question_stem: 1.2 BTC goes into a swap service at 10:00, and 1.19 BTC leaves it at 10:40 to a new address. What does the note write?
questions.correct_answer: The trace stops at the swap; the payout is a lead, Low, because only the amount and timing match.
incorrect_answers: The payout address is the same owner, Moderate, because the amounts differ by only the swap fee.
The trace continues to the new address, High, because both of its legs sit on the public Bitcoin ledger.
Nothing, because a swap through Monero erases both of the legs from the public chain for good.
questions.explanation: Both Bitcoin legs are visible and the middle is not. Pairing the two by amount and timing is Low, a lead for an agent and not a link the analyst asserts.

questions.question_stem: An exchange delisted Monero in early 2024. Why does that matter to an analyst writing up a 2023 case?
questions.correct_answer: Services keep deposit and withdrawal records, so the note states each service's policy as of the case's date.
incorrect_answers: The exchange deleted every Monero record when it delisted, so a 2023 trace has no lead there left to use.
The delisting makes any Monero deposit from before 2024 traceable, because the whole chain is rewritten.
The delisting shows the exchange was sanctioned, so each of its customers is a listed party as well.
questions.explanation: On- and off-ramps keep records whatever the chain hides, and policies change. The analyst names the last transparent transaction before the privacy coin and the first after it, with dates.

questions.question_stem: An analyst holds a Monero view key and sees 40 XMR arrive. What can the analyst say about the wallet?
questions.correct_answer: That 40 XMR arrived; spends do not show, so a balance from the key should not be relied upon.
incorrect_answers: That the wallet holds 40 XMR, because a view key shows every payment in and out of the wallet.
That the wallet spent 40 XMR, because a view key lists outgoing payments before it lists incoming.
That the analyst controls the wallet, because a view key can authorize spending from it.
questions.explanation: A Monero view key shows incoming transactions, not spends, and gives read access, not spend authority. The note says which key it was and what it covers.
questions.lesson_block: A view key shows payments in, not spends

questions.question_stem: How do Zcash's incoming viewing key and full viewing key differ?
questions.correct_answer: The incoming key shows payments in only; the full key shows payments in and out. Neither can spend.
incorrect_answers: The incoming key shows payments in and out; the full key adds the right to spend them as well as view them.
The incoming key shows the balance; the full key shows only the fees that the address has paid so far.
The incoming key works on t-addresses; the full key works on z-addresses and on t-addresses both of them.
questions.explanation: Viewing keys give read access, not spend authority. The note says which key it was and what it covers.

questions.question_stem: A Zcash round trip is matched by amount and timing, and the same exchange account is found at both ends. How is that rated, and why?
questions.correct_answer: High: the exchange account is a different kind of evidence, so two independent lines agree.
incorrect_answers: Moderate: a round trip and an account are two heuristics running over the same set of transactions.
Low: amount and timing are behavior only, and any line added to them is behavior as well.
Undetermined: Zcash hides its pool, so no pairing can be rated whatever else is found at the ends.
questions.explanation: High needs independent lines: a different kind of evidence, not a second heuristic over the same transactions. A round trip alone stays Low; which ring member was spent in today's Monero stays Undetermined.

questions.question_stem: A Monero input lists several earlier outputs instead of one. How does that hide which output was really spent?
questions.correct_answer: The signature proves one listed output was spent without showing which; the rest are decoys.
incorrect_answers: Each listed output is spent in part, so the amount is split evenly across all the members.
The listed outputs are encrypted, so only the receiver can later read which one was spent.
The real output is listed several times, so it hides among copies of itself in the ring.
questions.explanation: The assigned reading explains that a Cryptonote input names a set of earlier outputs, the real one among decoys (the paper calls them mixins), and carries a ring signature that is valid for one of them without revealing which. Privacy rests on the decoys being believable: if an observer can rule decoys out, the ring shrinks.

questions.question_stem: In early Monero, a ring of two lists outputs A and B. A month later, output A is spent by an input with no decoys. What does that reveal?
questions.correct_answer: That B was the real spend in the ring, because A was spent by the later input.
incorrect_answers: Nothing, because the open spend of A came after the ring had already been made.
That A and B share an owner, because both were listed together in the same ring.
That A was the real spend in the ring, and the later input spent it a second time.
questions.explanation: The assigned reading's chain reaction: an output known to be spent elsewhere can be struck off any ring that lists it as a decoy, leaving the other member as the real spend. The reading notes that order does not matter: a later open spend exposes an earlier ring just as well. This was a weakness of early Monero, which allowed inputs with no decoys.

questions.question_stem: Why did guessing the newest ring member so often find the real spend in the early Monero the reading studied?
questions.correct_answer: People tended to spend coins soon after getting them, while decoys were mostly older outputs.
incorrect_answers: Newer outputs carried larger amounts, so the biggest ring member was usually the real one.
Wallets could only pick decoys from blocks mined before the spender's own wallet had been made.
Only the newest ring member carried a key image, and that key image marked out the real spend.
questions.explanation: The assigned reading finds that real spends are usually recent, but early wallets drew decoys uniformly or from a triangular distribution that included much older outputs, so the real spend stood out as the newest. This describes early Monero: later versions changed how decoys are drawn, and the lesson says not to apply the guess to a later transaction without a newer study.

questions.specific_source_reading: quizes/lesson_synthesis/forensics_07-FO-privacy_coins-reading-synthesis.md: Mechanisms (Weakness 2: The Newest Member Is Usually Real); reading Sec. 1 Weakness 2 and Sec. 4.2

questions.question_stem: According to the reading, why does the chain reaction not work on RingCT transactions?
questions.correct_answer: RingCT came after the 2016 two-decoy minimum, so no output in its rings was ever spent decoy-free.
incorrect_answers: RingCT hides amounts, and striking off decoys needed amounts to match outputs to their spends.
RingCT drew decoys only from recent outputs, so no openly spent output could ever be listed in a ring.
RingCT dropped key images, so a spent output could no longer be matched to any later spend.
questions.explanation: The assigned reading says RingCT does not directly address traceability: its rings can list only RingCT outputs, and RingCT became valid after the network required at least two decoys, so none of those outputs was ever spent openly. The chain reaction therefore had nothing to start from. It was a weakness of Monero before 2017, since closed.
